Last verified against FDA and HHS primary sources: 2026-10-31. Federal compounding lists, advisory votes, and enforcement priorities change. This guide is educational pathway literacy, not legal advice.

The short version

  1. FDA approval of a finished drug is not the same as pharmacy compounding permission, and neither is the same as an online “research use only” (RUO) listing.
  2. Under section 503A, a bulk drug substance generally may be used in compounding only if it has an applicable USP/NF monograph, is a component of an FDA-approved drug, or appears on the 503A Bulks List established by FDA rulemaking.
  3. While that Bulks List is developed, FDA has used interim categories. Category 1 is the interim bucket associated with practical enforcement discretion for compounding evaluation. Category 2 flags significant safety-risk concerns (do-not-compound posture under the interim policy framing).
  4. Removal from Category 2 is not permission to compound. It does not place a substance on the Bulks List and does not equal Category 1.
  5. A Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (PCAC) recommendation is advisory. It is not a final FDA rule and does not by itself authorize compounding.
  6. As of 29 October 2026, peptides reviewed at the July 2026 PCAC meeting (including BPC-157 and TB-500) had not been added to the 503A Bulks List by FDA rulemaking. The codified 503A Bulks List does not name them, and no proposed rule to add them has appeared in the Federal Register. Treat any “now legal to compound” claim with extreme skepticism unless it cites a final listing.
  7. On 28 October 2026 the HHS Office of the Secretary announced a draft interim policy, the “Enforcement Discretion Policy Regarding 503A Compounding Using Certain Peptide Bulk Drug Substances” (FR Doc. 2026-22192; Docket No. HHS-OASH-2026-0496). The notice of availability was published in the Federal Register on 30 October 2026 at 91 FR 68526, and Regulations.gov lists the comment period as closing on 13 November 2026. It describes when HHS does not intend to take enforcement action against certain 503A compounding of six peptides. It is not FDA approval of any peptide, not a 503A Bulks List listing, and not binding. See the dated update below.

Update, October 2026: draft interim enforcement-discretion policy (published for comment)

As of 31 October 2026. This section records a draft interim policy published for comment. It describes what the published text says. It is not legal advice, and it will be revised when the record changes. For how compounded drugs differ from RUO-labelled peptides under the draft, see Compounded vs RUO Peptides; for a summary of the six-peptide policy, see the HHS 503A explainer.

What the primary documents say

  • The notice. The HHS Office of the Secretary filed a Federal Register notice of availability, FR Doc. 2026-22192 (Docket No. HHS-OASH-2026-0496; RIN 0910-ZD94), on 28 October 2026. It was published in the Federal Register on 30 October 2026 as 91 FR 68526 (pages 68526–68527): https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/10/30/2026-22192/enforcement-discretion-policy-regarding-503a-compounding-using-certain-peptide-bulk-drug-substances . The notice states: “HHS is announcing the availability of a draft ‘Enforcement Discretion Policy Regarding 503A Compounding Using Certain Peptide Bulk Drug Substances.’” It describes “the Secretary of HHS’s enforcement policy regarding the use of certain peptide bulk drug substances in compounding pursuant to section 503A … while the list of bulk drug substances that can be used in compounding under section 503A of the FD&C Act (the 503A bulks list) is developed through rulemaking.”
  • Comment window. “Written comments can be submitted until 2 weeks after date of publication in the Federal Register via regulations.gov on Docket No. HHS-OASH-2026-0496.” The notice itself prints no calendar date. The Regulations.gov entry for the notice (HHS-OASH-2026-0496-0002) lists the comment period as closing on 13 November 2026 at 11:59 pm Eastern Time, two weeks after publication: https://www.regulations.gov/commenton/HHS-OASH-2026-0496-0002 .
  • OIRA review concluded. OIRA’s EO 12866 review of “Interim Access Policy for Compounding Using Certain Peptides” (RIN 0910-ZD94) shows Concluded Date: 10/27/2026 and Concluded Action: Consistent with Change.
  • Which peptides. Appendix A lists six: BPC-157, epitalon, KPV, MOTS-c, semax, and TB-500.
  • What HHS says it will do. “Until a peptide bulk drug substance is addressed in a final rule as being included or not included on the 503A bulks list, HHS does not intend to take action against a State licensed pharmacy, Federal facility, or licensed physician compounding a drug product using a peptide bulk drug substance that is not a component of an FDA-approved drug product, the subject of an applicable USP or NF monograph, or on the 503A bulks list codified at 21 CFR 216.23(a), when all of the following circumstances are present.”

Scope and conditions (as written; not usage guidance)

The policy lists ten conditions. In summary:

  • Listed identity and route only (Appendix B). BPC-157 acetate (subcutaneous, intramuscular, oral, and topical dosage forms); TB-500 acetate, the fragment Ac-Leu-Lys-Lys-Thr-Glu-Thr-Gln-OH (subcutaneous or intramuscular injectable dosage forms); MOTS-c acetate (subcutaneous or intramuscular injectable dosage forms); epitalon acetate (subcutaneous or intramuscular injectable dosage forms dispensed in intermittent courses); semax free base (intranasal use); KPV acetate (topical and oral dosage forms). Other salt forms are outside the listed identities. This list describes the policy’s scope. It is not usage guidance.
  • Sourcing and testing. The bulk substance must come from a facility registered under section 510 with a valid certificate of analysis, and the original manufacturer must be FDA-registered and CGMP-compliant, with its location listed on the certificate.
  • Reporting and labeling. Compounders report products compounded, serious adverse events, and product quality issues to FDA and to the States, and report serious adverse events and product quality issues to FDA’s MedWatch program. Labels must include “This is a compounded drug product. Not for resale.”
  • Single ingredient. “The compounded drug product contains only a single Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient (API) listed in Appendix A.” Blends are outside the policy.
  • Other limits. Oral forms need documentation of adequate oral bioavailability in humans; the only co-packaged device may be an FDA 510(k)-cleared syringe; and section 503A’s insanitary-conditions and patient-specific prescription requirements still apply.

What it is not

  • Not an FDA approval. The notice states: “Compounded drugs are not FDA-approved, which means FDA does not review their safety, effectiveness, or quality before they are marketed.” The documents make no safety or efficacy finding for any of the six peptides.
  • Not a 503A Bulks List listing. None of the six is on 21 CFR 216.23(a). The notice says “FDA’s future rulemakings may propose adding some or all of these peptides to the 503A bulks list”; that rulemaking is still pending.
  • Not Category 1. None of the six is in any FDA interim category. HHS’s Appendix B says each was in Category 2 until 22 April 2026, and FDA’s categories list updated 14 May 2026 does not name them.
  • Not binding and not permanent. The notice says the draft policy “does not establish any rights for any person and is not binding on HHS or the public.” There is no calendar end date: it runs until a final rule addresses each peptide, and “HHS may revisit application of this interim policy (in whole or in part) if, among other things, a safety signal or product quality issue arises.”
  • Not a change to RUO status. HHS states that the policy is meant to “discourage the continued, widespread use of certain research-use-only peptides supplied by foreign manufacturers that pose a safety risk to US patients.” Nothing in the policy treats research-use-only products as covered.
  • Advisory votes are still advisory. For each peptide, Appendix B states that FDA’s Center for Drug Evaluation and Research (CDER) recommended against listing and that the PCAC voted in favor. FDA has not posted vote results on its meeting page, and this guide gives no vote counts.

Petition, state law and the next PCAC meeting (as of 31 October 2026)

  • A citizen petition, not a lawsuit. On 23 October 2026 the Partnership for Safe Medicines (PSM) filed a citizen petition with FDA under 21 C.F.R. § 10.30 (Docket No. FDA-2026-P-13366). It asks FDA to “refrain from taking action, whether through regulation, addition to ‘Category 1’ … or otherwise through exercise of enforcement discretion or any other action, to allow for compounding of drug products using any of the seven peptide bulk drug substances” considered at the July 23–24, 2026 PCAC meeting. Because PSM argues that the July committee “was constituted in violation of the Federal Advisory Committee Act (‘FACA’) and the Ethics in Government Act (‘EIGA’)”, it also asks FDA to “refrain from relying on it”. PSM’s press release describes this as urging FDA “to disregard the advisory committee vote that recommended allowing them.” The petition was filed before HHS announced its policy. A citizen petition is a request to the agency. It is not litigation and not a ruling, and these sources report no FDA response. The FACA and ethics points are PSM’s arguments, not findings.
  • States may not follow. AJMC reports that Jeff Cohen, cofounder of the American Peptide Association, told Reuters that the move could heighten tension between federal and state regulators and that states may not follow the federal government in relaxing rules. That is a reported comment, not a legal conclusion. The HHS notice is a federal enforcement policy and does not itself state how any state will act.
  • Five more peptides at the next PCAC meeting (before the end of February 2027). AJMC reports that, as of July, the PCAC was scheduled to review five more unapproved peptides for pharmacy compounding in February. FDA’s PCAC meeting page says FDA “will host an advisory committee meeting before the end of February 2027” and lists five bulk drug substances (see the next-PCAC note below). A scheduled review is not a listing and not permission to compound.

Earlier reporting, and by whom

  • Washington Post, 7 October 2026. Rachel Roubein reported, citing two people familiar with the matter who spoke on condition of anonymity, that the administration was crafting plans to allow the temporary sale of certain previously restricted peptides through some compounding pharmacies while regulations are developed. That report predates the published text.
  • Holland & Knight, 16 October 2026. In a client alert written before the text was released, the law firm Holland & Knight (Sarah Starling Crossan and Shalyn Watkins) wrote that “the most likely approach of the policy is interim enforcement discretion.” This is one law firm’s analysis of a then-unpublished document, not HHS’s description of it.

Definitions and COA literacy live in the beginner’s guide to research peptides. On-site context for the 2026 category headlines is FDA peptide reclassification 2026: what researchers need to know, which separates Category 2 removal from Category 1 and from the Bulks List. Verify every status claim against current FDA primary pages—interim categories, withdrawn nominations, and final Bulks List rulemaking are easy to conflate in secondary summaries.

How 503A compounding lists actually work

Section 503A of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act governs traditional patient-specific compounding by state-licensed pharmacies (high level). FDA’s compounding pages explain that bulk drug substances used under 503A are limited. In plain language, a substance generally needs one of these pathways:

  • An applicable USP or NF monograph, or
  • Being a component of an FDA-approved drug, or
  • Appearing on FDA’s 503A Bulks List (built through agency evaluation / rulemaking)

Section 503B covers outsourcing facilities that register with FDA and face different bulk-substance and quality rules (including a separate 503B bulks / clinical-need framework and shortage-related pathways). This guide focuses on the 503A literacy most readers mean when they ask about “compounded peptides,” without turning into a full pharmacy-law manual.

Interim categories (why “Category 2” dominates headlines)

While formal bulks lists are developed, FDA has sorted nominated substances into interim categories. Educational explainers (including clinic/legal trackers) commonly describe:

  • Category 1 — substances under evaluation where FDA may exercise enforcement discretion; the only interim category that carries practical compounding consideration in that framing. Category 1 is still not FDA drug approval and is not, by itself, a license to compound.
  • Category 2 — substances FDA has identified as raising significant safety risks; do-not-compound posture under the interim policy
  • Category 3 — nominations lacking adequate supporting information (where that category is used)
  • Withdrawn nominations — a separate posture: nominators withdrew a nomination. Being “withdrawn” / off Category 2 is not permission

Two details from FDA’s 503A pages (503A page content current as of 14 May 2026) matter for the October 2026 news. First, FDA’s guidance “does not intend to place bulk drug substances nominated on or after January 7, 2025, into these categories.” Second, FDA’s 503A categories list, updated 14 May 2026, shows GHK-Cu (except for injectable routes of administration) added back to Category 1 after a nominator clarified its withdrawal. That is an interim enforcement-discretion posture with conditions, not FDA approval and not a Bulks List listing. Injectable GHK-Cu remains in the withdrawn-nomination table.

FDA also publishes a page on bulk substances that may present significant safety risks, including substances still listed under Category 2 and a table of substances whose nominations were withdrawn (with narrative safety concerns retained for context)—including entries such as BPC-157 and thymosin beta-4 fragment (LKKTETQ), also known as TB-500.

The distinction almost everyone gets wrong

In 2026, FDA actions that removed certain peptides from Category 2 (including via withdrawn nominations) were widely reported as those peptides “becoming legal again.” That is not what Category 2 removal means.

  • Off Category 2 ≠ on the 503A Bulks List
  • Off Category 2 ≠ Category 1
  • Off Category 2 ≠ automatic lawful compounding under 503A

A peptide can therefore be off Category 2 and still not lawfully compoundable under the interim framework—which is the situation many popular research peptides have been in while PCAC review and rulemaking continue.

What PCAC did—and did not do—in July 2026

On 23–24 July 2026, FDA’s Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee reviewed several nominated peptide bulk substances for possible 503A Bulks List inclusion. Reporting on the meeting (including BMJ coverage and legal analyses) describes committee votes that recommended inclusion for multiple peptides such as BPC-157 and TB-500, while FDA staff briefing materials had argued against inclusion for the set under review.

Critical literacy points:

  • PCAC votes are advisory and non-binding
  • FDA still decides whether/how to add a substance to the Bulks List
  • Addition generally requires notice-and-comment rulemaking
  • A favorable vote is not marketing approval as a drug
  • A favorable vote is not, by itself, a green light to compound

Status note (Harvard Chan, 1 October 2026; rechecked 29 October 2026). In a Q&A published by Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, Professor S. Bryn Austin said FDA “has not yet announced if it will accept or reject the committee’s recommendation” from the July Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee vote on allowing compounders to manufacture and sell several synthetic peptides. As of 29 October 2026, no proposed rule to add any of these peptides to the Bulks List has appeared in the Federal Register. The draft interim enforcement-discretion policy that the HHS Office of the Secretary announced on 28 October 2026 and published in the Federal Register on 30 October 2026 at 91 FR 68526 (see the October 2026 update above) is an HHS enforcement policy, not FDA approval and not a Bulks List rule. Austin’s statement is a status report, not a legal conclusion and not permission to compound. A PCAC vote is still advisory. It is not a final FDA rule, not FDA drug approval, and not placement on the 503A Bulks List. Removal from Category 2 remains not permission to compound. Source: Karen Feldscher, “Peptides are all over social media and the news. Here’s what to know about them,” Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, 1 October 2026, https://hsph.harvard.edu/news/peptides-are-all-over-social-media-and-the-news-heres-what-to-know-about-them/

Next PCAC discussion (FDA page, read 3 October 2026; unchanged when rechecked 31 October 2026). FDA’s Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee meeting page states that FDA “will host an advisory committee meeting before the end of February 2027.” The agenda on that page lists these bulk drug substances for discussion for possible inclusion on the 503A Bulks List: cathelicidin (LL-37), GHK-Cu, dihexa acetate, melanotan II, and mechano growth factor, pegylated (PEG-MGF). The same page says advisory-committee recommendations are non-binding. A scheduled discussion is not a Bulks List listing and is not permission to compound. The page does not list non-pegylated MGF as a separate substance. It says FDA “intends to publish a Federal Register notice and establish a docket for public comment on this meeting in the near future.” As of 31 October 2026 no Federal Register notice for that February 2027 meeting was found. That meeting notice is separate from the HHS notice at 91 FR 68526 (Docket No. HHS-OASH-2026-0496), which has been published. Source: https://www.fda.gov/advisory-committees/pharmacy-compounding-advisory-committee/meeting-pharmacy-compounding-advisory-committee

Until a substance actually appears on the applicable final list (or otherwise qualifies under the statute), educational status trackers have summarized many of these peptides as not currently compoundable under 503A—regardless of supplier or clinic marketing.

Example: BPC-157 and similar peptides (primary-supported only)

Use these as illustrations of pathway confusion, not as a complete legality chart.

What “research use only” means—and does not

RUO / “not for human consumption” is a labeling and marketing posture. Legitimate laboratories do need research reagents. That is real.

What RUO does not automatically do:

  • Create FDA approval
  • Place a substance on a compounding bulks list
  • Guarantee purity, sterility, or correct identity
  • Erase FDA’s ability to evaluate intended use from the totality of marketing

Under 21 CFR 201.128, “intended uses” are based on objective intent—expressions, design/composition, and circumstances of distribution—including labeling claims and advertising. FDA warning letters to peptide sellers have treated website disease/structure-function style claims as evidence that products are being marketed as drugs, and then as unapproved new drugs when no approval is in effect—regardless of research branding.

The 24 August 2026 FDA warning letter to Peptide Partners LLC says this directly about that firm’s labeled products: despite statements marketing them “for research use only” and “not for human or veterinary use,” website evidence established that the products were intended to be drugs for human use. RUO wording on those products did not prevent the unapproved-new-drug finding in that letter. This is an enforcement example, not a complete list of every August 2026 letter and not legal advice about any other seller.

High-level takeaway: legality depends on pathway and marketing context, not on a disclaimer sticker. Static “legal or illegal” charts go stale quickly; prefer FDA primary pages and dated trackers over slogans.

FAQs

Are research peptides legal to buy online?

There is no single yes/no answer for every peptide, seller, claim, and jurisdiction. RUO listings exist; FDA still polices unapproved new drugs marketed for human use. This page does not advise purchases.

Does “removed from Category 2” mean pharmacies can compound it?

No. Removal from Category 2 is not placement on the 503A Bulks List and is not Category 1 permission.

Did PCAC “approve” BPC-157 or TB-500 in July 2026?

No. PCAC votes are non-binding recommendations. FDA’s briefing documents proposed that BPC-157 and TB-500 not be included, and the HHS policy’s Appendix B states that the committee voted in favor. A vote is not FDA drug approval and not a final bulks-list rule.

Did FDA approve compounded peptides in October 2026?

No. On 28 October 2026 the HHS Office of the Secretary announced a draft interim enforcement-discretion policy published for comment (FR Doc. 2026-22192). FDA rulemaking on the Bulks List is still pending.

Is compounding the same as FDA approval?

No. Compounding is a limited pharmacy pathway. Approval is a separate product authorization process.

Does WADA ban mean something is illegal for everyone?

No. WADA governs athletes in anti-doping programs. It is separate from FDA compounding and general consumer law—though the same substance can be constrained in multiple systems at once.

How 503A compounding lists actually work

Section 503A of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act governs traditional patient-specific compounding by state-licensed pharmacies (high level). FDA’s compounding pages explain that bulk drug substances used under 503A are limited. In plain language, a substance generally needs one of these pathways:

  • An applicable USP or NF monograph, or
  • Being a component of an FDA-approved drug, or
  • Appearing on FDA’s 503A Bulks List (built through agency evaluation / rulemaking)

Section 503B covers outsourcing facilities that register with FDA and face different bulk-substance and quality rules (including a separate 503B bulks / clinical-need framework and shortage-related pathways). This guide focuses on the 503A literacy most readers mean when they ask about “compounded peptides,” without turning into a full pharmacy-law manual.

Interim categories (why “Category 2” dominates headlines)

While formal bulks lists are developed, FDA has sorted nominated substances into interim categories. Educational explainers (including clinic/legal trackers) commonly describe:

  • Category 1 — substances under evaluation where FDA may exercise enforcement discretion; the only interim category that carries practical compounding consideration in that framing. Category 1 is still not FDA drug approval and is not, by itself, a license to compound.
  • Category 2 — substances FDA has identified as raising significant safety risks; do-not-compound posture under the interim policy
  • Category 3 — nominations lacking adequate supporting information (where that category is used)
  • Withdrawn nominations — a separate posture: nominators withdrew a nomination. Being “withdrawn” / off Category 2 is not permission

Two details from FDA’s 503A pages (503A page content current as of 14 May 2026) matter for the October 2026 news. First, FDA’s guidance “does not intend to place bulk drug substances nominated on or after January 7, 2025, into these categories.” Second, FDA’s 503A categories list, updated 14 May 2026, shows GHK-Cu (except for injectable routes of administration) added back to Category 1 after a nominator clarified its withdrawal. That is an interim enforcement-discretion posture with conditions, not FDA approval and not a Bulks List listing. Injectable GHK-Cu remains in the withdrawn-nomination table.

FDA also publishes a page on bulk substances that may present significant safety risks, including substances still listed under Category 2 and a table of substances whose nominations were withdrawn (with narrative safety concerns retained for context)—including entries such as BPC-157 and thymosin beta-4 fragment (LKKTETQ), also known as TB-500.

The distinction almost everyone gets wrong

In 2026, FDA actions that removed certain peptides from Category 2 (including via withdrawn nominations) were widely reported as those peptides “becoming legal again.” That is not what Category 2 removal means.

  • Off Category 2 ≠ on the 503A Bulks List
  • Off Category 2 ≠ Category 1
  • Off Category 2 ≠ automatic lawful compounding under 503A

A peptide can therefore be off Category 2 and still not lawfully compoundable under the interim framework—which is the situation many popular research peptides have been in while PCAC review and rulemaking continue.

What PCAC did—and did not do—in July 2026

On 23–24 July 2026, FDA’s Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee reviewed several nominated peptide bulk substances for possible 503A Bulks List inclusion. Reporting on the meeting (including BMJ coverage and legal analyses) describes committee votes that recommended inclusion for multiple peptides such as BPC-157 and TB-500, while FDA staff briefing materials had argued against inclusion for the set under review.

Critical literacy points:

  • PCAC votes are advisory and non-binding
  • FDA still decides whether/how to add a substance to the Bulks List
  • Addition generally requires notice-and-comment rulemaking
  • A favorable vote is not marketing approval as a drug
  • A favorable vote is not, by itself, a green light to compound

Status note (Harvard Chan, 1 October 2026; rechecked 29 October 2026). In a Q&A published by Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, Professor S. Bryn Austin said FDA “has not yet announced if it will accept or reject the committee’s recommendation” from the July Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee vote on allowing compounders to manufacture and sell several synthetic peptides. As of 29 October 2026, no proposed rule to add any of these peptides to the Bulks List has appeared in the Federal Register. The draft interim enforcement-discretion policy that the HHS Office of the Secretary published for comment on 28 October 2026 (see the October 2026 update above) is an HHS enforcement policy, not FDA approval and not a Bulks List rule. Austin’s statement is a status report, not a legal conclusion and not permission to compound. A PCAC vote is still advisory. It is not a final FDA rule, not FDA drug approval, and not placement on the 503A Bulks List. Removal from Category 2 remains not permission to compound. Source: Karen Feldscher, “Peptides are all over social media and the news. Here’s what to know about them,” Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, 1 October 2026, https://hsph.harvard.edu/news/peptides-are-all-over-social-media-and-the-news-heres-what-to-know-about-them/

Next PCAC discussion (FDA page, read 3 October 2026; unchanged when rechecked 29 October 2026). FDA’s Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee meeting page states that FDA “will host an advisory committee meeting before the end of February 2027.” The agenda on that page lists these bulk drug substances for discussion for possible inclusion on the 503A Bulks List: cathelicidin (LL-37), GHK-Cu, dihexa acetate, melanotan II, and mechano growth factor, pegylated (PEG-MGF). The same page says advisory-committee recommendations are non-binding. A scheduled discussion is not a Bulks List listing and is not permission to compound. The page does not list non-pegylated MGF as a separate substance, and it says a Federal Register notice and public-comment docket are still forthcoming. Source: https://www.fda.gov/advisory-committees/pharmacy-compounding-advisory-committee/meeting-pharmacy-compounding-advisory-committee

Until a substance actually appears on the applicable final list (or otherwise qualifies under the statute), educational status trackers have summarized many of these peptides as not currently compoundable under 503A—regardless of supplier or clinic marketing.

Example: BPC-157 and similar peptides (primary-supported only)

Use these as illustrations of pathway confusion, not as a complete legality chart.

BPC-157

  • Not an FDA-approved drug for human use (FDA Approved Drugs database does not list it; DoD OPSS describes it as an unapproved drug).
  • Appears in FDA’s compounding safety-risk materials (including withdrawn-nomination / safety-narrative context regarding immunogenicity, peptide impurities/API characterization, and limited human safety information for proposed routes). That withdrawn / off Category 2 framing is not “placed in Category 1.”
  • July 2026 PCAC reporting: committee recommended 503A Bulks List inclusion; recommendation ≠ final listing.
  • WADA 2026 Prohibited List: named under S0 Non-approved substances (prohibited at all times)—sport rules, not a substitute for FDA compounding analysis.
  • DoD OPSS: listed among prohibited dietary supplement ingredients for service members; research-chemical labeling does not change that workplace guidance.
  • Encyclopedia illustration only: BPC-157.

TB-500 (thymosin β4 fragment LKKTETQ)

  • Not an FDA-approved drug for injectable injury use.
  • FDA safety-risk materials discuss the fragment and note lack of identified human exposure data for that fragment in FDA’s summary.
  • July 2026 PCAC reporting: recommended for inclusion (advisory).
  • WADA: thymosin-β4 and derivatives e.g. TB-500 named under S2.3 (prohibited at all times).
  • Encyclopedia illustration only: TB-500.

What this example is not saying

It is not a green light, a ban list for personal possession in every jurisdiction, or legal advice about buying/selling. It shows why RUO websites, compounding clinics, and approved drugs are different conversations.

For evidence (not law) on BPC-157 vs TB-500, see what the evidence actually shows. A side-by-side comparison lives at compare marketplace listings.

What “research use only” means—and does not

RUO / “not for human consumption” is a labeling and marketing posture. Legitimate laboratories do need research reagents. That is real.

What RUO does not automatically do:

  • Create FDA approval
  • Place a substance on a compounding bulks list
  • Guarantee purity, sterility, or correct identity
  • Erase FDA’s ability to evaluate intended use from the totality of marketing

Under 21 CFR 201.128, “intended uses” are based on objective intent—expressions, design/composition, and circumstances of distribution—including labeling claims and advertising. FDA warning letters to peptide sellers have treated website disease/structure-function style claims as evidence that products are being marketed as drugs, and then as unapproved new drugs when no approval is in effect—regardless of research branding.

The 24 August 2026 FDA warning letter to Peptide Partners LLC says this directly about that firm’s labeled products: despite statements marketing them “for research use only” and “not for human or veterinary use,” website evidence established that the products were intended to be drugs for human use. RUO wording on those products did not prevent the unapproved-new-drug finding in that letter. This is an enforcement example, not a complete list of every August 2026 letter and not legal advice about any other seller.

High-level takeaway: legality depends on pathway and marketing context, not on a disclaimer sticker. Static “legal or illegal” charts go stale quickly; prefer FDA primary pages and dated trackers over slogans.

WADA / sport (briefly)

Anti-doping rules are not general criminal law and are not FDA compounding law. Athletes subject to testing follow the WADA Prohibited List (and their sport’s program). As of the 2026 list:

  • BPC-157 — S0 (named example)
  • Thymosin-β4 and derivatives e.g. TB-500 — S2.3

A blend containing a prohibited substance is still a sport risk. Check the current list; it updates annually.

Practical literacy checklist (not legal advice)

  1. Is there an FDA-approved finished drug for this exact product/use?
  2. If compounded: does it qualify under 503A/503B pathways today (monograph, approved-drug component, or final bulks listing—not vibes)? Category 1 is interim enforcement discretion, not a qualifying pathway or a listing.
  3. Was a headline about Category 2 removal or a PCAC vote being treated as if it were a final rule?
  4. Is an online seller making drug claims while waving an RUO disclaimer?
  5. Do sport / DoD / employer rules separately restrict the substance?
  6. When in doubt: current FDA pages + qualified counsel—not forums.

FAQs

Are research peptides legal to buy online?

There is no single yes/no answer for every peptide, seller, claim, and jurisdiction. RUO listings exist; FDA still polices unapproved new drugs marketed for human use. This page does not advise purchases.

Does “removed from Category 2” mean pharmacies can compound it?

No. Removal from Category 2 is not placement on the 503A Bulks List and is not Category 1 permission.

Did PCAC “approve” BPC-157 or TB-500 in July 2026?

No. PCAC votes are non-binding recommendations. FDA’s briefing documents proposed that BPC-157 and TB-500 not be included, and the HHS policy’s Appendix B states that the committee voted in favor. A vote is not FDA drug approval and not a final bulks-list rule.

Did FDA approve compounded peptides in October 2026?

No. On 28 October 2026 the HHS Office of the Secretary announced a draft interim enforcement-discretion policy published for comment (FR Doc. 2026-22192). It describes when HHS does not intend to take action against certain 503A compounding of six peptides under listed conditions. It is not FDA drug approval, it does not place any peptide on the 503A Bulks List or in Category 1, it is not binding, and it makes no safety or efficacy finding. FDA rulemaking on the Bulks List is still pending.

Is compounding the same as FDA approval?

No. Compounding is a limited pharmacy pathway. Approval is a separate product authorization process.

Does WADA ban mean something is illegal for everyone?

No. WADA governs athletes in anti-doping programs. It is separate from FDA compounding and general consumer law—though the same substance can be constrained in multiple systems at once.

Where should I check status before believing a clinic ad?

FDA compounding / bulks / safety-risk pages first; then dated educational trackers; then counsel. On-site Peptidemap posts are context only—cross-check against primary FDA sources when making decisions.

Peptidemap is a research-use-only (RUO) comparison publisher. It is not a clinic, pharmacy, supplier or drug company. This page explains a regulatory document. It is not medical, legal or purchasing advice, and it does not say that any compounded or RUO product is safe, effective or legal to use.

On 28 Oct 2026 the HHS Office of the Secretary announced a draft "Enforcement Discretion Policy Regarding 503A Compounding Using Certain Peptide Bulk Drug Substances" [1][2] [primary]. It names six peptides: BPC-157, epitalon, KPV, MOTS-c, semax and TB-500 [1] [primary]. The Federal Register notice (FR Doc. 2026-22192, docket HHS-OASH-2026-0496, RIN 0910-ZD94) was filed on 28 Oct and published on 30 Oct 2026 at 91 FR 68526 [2] [primary]. This guide covers who can compound, what the draft does and does not do, and how compounded drugs differ from RUO-labelled peptides.

Who can compound: 503A vs 503B

Compounding is described in the notice as "a practice in which a licensed pharmacist, a licensed physician or, in the case of an outsourcing facility, a person under the supervision of a licensed pharmacist, combines, mixes or alters ingredients of a drug to create a medication tailored to the needs of an individual patient" [2] [primary].

Federal law has two compounding tracks:

  • Section 503A covers drugs compounded "by a licensed pharmacist in a State-licensed pharmacy or Federal facility, or by a licensed physician" [1] [primary]. If certain conditions are met, those drugs are exempt from FDA pre-market approval, the "adequate directions for use" labelling rule, and federal CGMP requirements [1] [primary]. One condition is that each drug must be compounded "based on the receipt of a valid patient specific prescription" [1] [primary]. Another condition limits which bulk ingredients can be used. The ingredient must have a USP or NF monograph, or be a component of an FDA-approved drug, or appear on the 503A Bulks List, which is set through rulemaking [1] [primary].
  • Section 503B covers outsourcing facilities. These are the larger facilities that NPR describes as "producing higher volumes of medicines" [5] [press].

The draft is written for 503A. It names "a State-licensed pharmacy, Federal facility, or licensed physician" as the entities it covers [1] [primary]. Outsourcing facilities are not among the entities it names. NPR reports that the policy "doesn't apply to the larger ones, called 503Bs" [5] [press]. NCPA describes the policy as covering 503A compounding pharmacies [6] [press].

What enforcement discretion does and does NOT mean

The core sentence of the draft says that, in the listed circumstances, "HHS does not intend to take enforcement action against a State-licensed pharmacy, Federal facility, or licensed physician compounding a drug product using a bulk drug substance in Appendix A" [1] [primary].

The documents say this is not:

  • Approval. "Compounded drugs are not FDA-approved, which means FDA does not review their safety, effectiveness, or quality before they are marketed" [1][2] [primary]. HHS cites "the lack of availability of approved products" [2] [primary].
  • A Bulks List listing. The draft applies to substances that are not "on the 503A bulks list codified at 21 CFR 216.23(a)" [1] [primary]. It states that "FDA's future rulemakings may propose adding some or all of these peptides" [2] [primary]. NCPA reports that pharmacies "are still awaiting final rulemaking" [6] [press].
  • Category 1. Appendix B says each of the six was in FDA's interim Category 2 from 2023 "until April 22, 2026" [1] [primary]. None is in Category 1. The HHS draft is a separate policy.
  • Binding or permanent. The notice says the draft "does not establish any rights for any person and is not binding on HHS or the public" [2] [primary]. It gives no end date. It applies "until a peptide bulk drug substance is addressed in a final rule as being included or not included on the 503A bulks list" [1] [primary]. NCPA notes that "no timeframe was given" [6] [press].
  • Irrevocable. "HHS may revisit application of this interim policy (in whole or in part) if, among other things, a safety signal or product quality issue arises" [1][2] [primary].
  • A safety or efficacy finding. The documents contain no determination that any of the six is safe or effective. Appendix B records that for each peptide "CDER recommended against listing" and that the PCAC, which met 23–24 Jul 2026 [4], voted in favour [1] [primary]. The draft was reviewed by OIRA from 14 Oct to 27 Oct 2026 under the title "Interim Access Policy for Compounding Using Certain Peptides" [3] [primary]. NPR reports that FDA's own scientists recommended against unwinding the restrictions [5] [press].

The comment window is "2 weeks after date of publication in the Federal Register," through regulations.gov on docket HHS-OASH-2026-0496 [2] [primary]. Regulations.gov lists the comment period as closing on 13 Nov 2026 at 11:59 pm Eastern Time [10] [primary].

Scope: forms, listed routes and single ingredient

The coverage is narrow. Appendix B defines each covered identity by amino acid sequence, formula and molecular weight [1] [primary]. The forms are BPC-157 acetate, TB-500 acetate, epitalon acetate, KPV acetate, MOTS-c acetate and semax free base. Other salt forms are not listed.

The draft also lists routes. The list below describes the policy's scope only. It is not usage information.

  • BPC-157 acetate: subcutaneous, intramuscular, oral and topical dosage forms
  • TB-500 acetate: subcutaneous or intramuscular injectable dosage forms only
  • MOTS-c acetate: subcutaneous or intramuscular injectable dosage forms
  • Epitalon acetate: subcutaneous or intramuscular injectable dosage forms "dispensed in intermittent courses"
  • Semax free base: intranasal use
  • KPV acetate: topical and oral dosage forms [1] [primary]

The product must contain "only a single Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient (API) listed in Appendix A" [1] [primary]. Blends fall outside the draft. That includes combinations of two listed peptides, such as BPC-157 with TB-500. The only drug delivery device that may be co-packaged with or contain the compounded drug is "an FDA 510(k)-cleared syringe" [1] [primary]. For any oral form, the compounder is expected to keep documentation showing "an adequate level of oral bioavailability in humans" [1] [primary].

Identity, purity and adverse-event conditions, as stated

The draft does not use the word "certify." These are the conditions in its own words [1] [primary]:

  • Identity. The substance "has the identity and limitations in route of administration described in Appendix B. The identity includes but is not limited to amino acid sequence, chemical structure, molecular weight, and molecular formula."
  • Characterization. The substance "is from a facility registered under section 510 … and characterized and identified in a valid certificate of analysis (COA) that includes test results consistent with existing guidance-based criteria described by FDA." HHS says this "helps provide assurance that what a compounder receives from a supplier is what it claims to be and has been tested for identity, purity, potency, and the absence of harmful contaminants such as endotoxins, heavy metals, microbial contamination, and impurities."
  • Original manufacturer. The original manufacturer, "not a subsequent packer, repacker, labeler, or distributor," must be registered under section 510 and comply with CGMP. Its facility location must be listed on the COA. An FDA-registered repacker or reseller must itself document "vendor validation" of the manufacturer and its COA. The COA requirements include the grade "Intended for human drug compounding."
  • Reporting. Compounders must "report products compounded, serious adverse events, and product quality issues to FDA and to the States where the products are compounded and sent (if different)." Serious adverse events must be reported "regardless of whether or not considered drug related," and product-quality issues as well, to FDA's MedWatch program. Product reports must include the active ingredient and its strength, the original manufacturer with its facility identifier, and the dosage form and route. The reporting procedure "should be detailed on the product labeling provided to the patient."
  • Label. The label must state: "This is a compounded drug product. Not for resale."
  • Other law. The product must comply with "all other applicable requirements of the FD&C Act," including the insanitary-conditions ban and "section 503A's … patient specific prescription requirement."

How this differs from RUO-labelled products

RUO ("research use only") products are sold with a label saying they are not for human use. The draft's conditions describe a different channel:

  • Labelling. Covered compounded products carry the statement "This is a compounded drug product. Not for resale" [1] [primary]. RUO products carry research-only labelling.
  • Intended use. The draft covers drug products compounded for an individual patient under section 503A [1] [primary]. RUO labelling states that a product is not intended for human use.
  • Prescription. The draft requires a valid patient-specific prescription [1] [primary]. No prescription is involved in RUO sales.
  • Identity and purity oversight. The draft ties coverage to a 510-registered, CGMP-compliant original manufacturer, a COA meeting FDA-referenced testing criteria, and MedWatch reporting [1] [primary]. RUO products are outside these terms, and none of the draft's identity, purity or reporting conditions apply to them.

HHS's stated rationale refers to RUO directly. The Secretary "has determined that this limited enforcement-discretion policy will discourage the continued, widespread use of certain research-use-only peptides supplied by foreign manufacturers that pose a safety risk to US patients" [1] [primary]. That is HHS's framing. The draft does not cover, authorise or legitimise RUO sales.

State-law note

The draft mentions States in its reporting condition and covers "State-licensed" pharmacies [1] [primary]. It contains no express statement about state pharmacy law. The law firm Frier Levitt writes that the policy "does not displace independent state pharmacy board requirements" and that pharmacies must still assess state law [7] [press]. That is the firm's analysis, not text from the policy. AJMC reports that Jeff Cohen, cofounder of the American Peptide Association, told Reuters that states may not follow the federal government in relaxing rules [11] [press]. That is a reported comment, not a statement of any state's position.

Petition and next PCAC review

On 23 Oct 2026 the Partnership for Safe Medicines (PSM) filed a citizen petition with FDA (docket FDA-2026-P-13366) [12] [primary, petitioner's filing]. It asks FDA to "refrain from taking action … to allow for compounding of drug products using any of the seven peptide bulk drug substances" considered at the 23–24 Jul 2026 PCAC meeting, and to "refrain from relying on" that meeting, which PSM says was constituted in violation of federal advisory-committee and ethics law [12]. PSM's press release describes this as urging FDA "to disregard the advisory committee vote that recommended allowing them" [13] [press release]. It is a petition to the agency, not a lawsuit, and no FDA response is reported in these sources.

AJMC reports that, as of July, the PCAC was scheduled to review five more unapproved peptides for pharmacy compounding in February [11] [press]. FDA's PCAC page says FDA "will host an advisory committee meeting before the end of February 2027" [14] [primary]. A scheduled review is not a listing.

Litigation context: Eli Lilly's retatrutide suits

On 12 Aug 2026, Eli Lilly announced six US lawsuits over unapproved retatrutide. Retatrutide is an investigational drug that Lilly says is in Phase 3 trials and not approved anywhere [8] [company-reported]. Lilly says the suits target "compounding pharmacies, medical spas, and online sellers that falsely claim their drugs are for 'research-use only' when they are actually intended for human use" [8] [company-reported]. The six cases it lists were filed in federal district courts in California and Texas [8] [company-reported]. Reuters reported the filings the same day [9] [press]. These are allegations, and no ruling is reported in these sources. Retatrutide is not one of the six peptides in the HHS draft.

FAQ

Did FDA approve these six peptides?

No. The notice comes from the HHS Office of the Secretary. It says compounded drugs are not FDA-approved, and none of the six is on the 503A Bulks List [1][2] [primary].

Is the policy final?

No. The Federal Register notice calls it a draft, says it is not binding, and opens a two-week comment window after publication on 30 Oct 2026 [2] [primary].

How long does it last?

No end date is given. It applies until a final rule addresses each substance, and HHS may revisit it at any time [1] [primary].

Does it cover blends such as BPC-157 with TB-500?

No. The draft requires a single listed active ingredient [1] [primary].

Does it cover RUO-labelled products?

No. Its terms depend on 503A compounding, a patient-specific prescription and registered CGMP sourcing. HHS calls foreign RUO peptides a safety risk [1] [primary].

Did FDA scientists support it?

Appendix B records that CDER recommended against listing each of the six and that the PCAC voted in favour [1] [primary].

On 28 Oct 2026 the HHS Office of the Secretary announced a draft "Enforcement Discretion Policy Regarding 503A Compounding Using Certain Peptide Bulk Drug Substances" [1][2] [primary]. It names six peptides: BPC-157, epitalon, KPV, MOTS-c, semax and TB-500 [1] [primary]. The Federal Register notice (FR Doc. 2026-22192, docket HHS-OASH-2026-0496, RIN 0910-ZD94) was filed on 28 Oct and is scheduled for publication on 30 Oct 2026 [2] [primary]. This guide covers who can compound, what the draft does and does not do, and how compounded drugs differ from RUO-labelled peptides.

Who can compound: 503A vs 503B

Compounding is described in the notice as "a practice in which a licensed pharmacist, a licensed physician or, in the case of an outsourcing facility, a person under the supervision of a licensed pharmacist, combines, mixes or alters ingredients of a drug to create a medication tailored to the needs of an individual patient" [2] [primary].

Federal law has two compounding tracks:

  • Section 503A covers drugs compounded "by a licensed pharmacist in a State-licensed pharmacy or Federal facility, or by a licensed physician" [1] [primary]. If certain conditions are met, those drugs are exempt from FDA pre-market approval, the "adequate directions for use" labelling rule, and federal CGMP requirements [1] [primary]. One condition is that each drug must be compounded "based on the receipt of a valid patient specific prescription" [1] [primary]. Another condition limits which bulk ingredients can be used. The ingredient must have a USP or NF monograph, or be a component of an FDA-approved drug, or appear on the 503A Bulks List, which is set through rulemaking [1] [primary].
  • Section 503B covers outsourcing facilities. These are the larger facilities that NPR describes as "producing higher volumes of medicines" [5] [press].

The draft is written for 503A. It names "a State-licensed pharmacy, Federal facility, or licensed physician" as the entities it covers [1] [primary]. Outsourcing facilities are not among the entities it names. NPR reports that the policy "doesn't apply to the larger ones, called 503Bs" [5] [press]. NCPA describes the policy as covering 503A compounding pharmacies [6] [press].

What enforcement discretion does and does NOT mean

The core sentence of the draft says that, in the listed circumstances, "HHS does not intend to take enforcement action against a State-licensed pharmacy, Federal facility, or licensed physician compounding a drug product using a bulk drug substance in Appendix A" [1] [primary].

The documents say this is not:

  • Approval. "Compounded drugs are not FDA-approved, which means FDA does not review their safety, effectiveness, or quality before they are marketed" [1][2] [primary]. HHS cites "the lack of availability of approved products" [2] [primary].
  • A Bulks List listing. The draft applies to substances that are not "on the 503A bulks list codified at 21 CFR 216.23(a)" [1] [primary]. It states that "FDA's future rulemakings may propose adding some or all of these peptides" [2] [primary]. NCPA reports that pharmacies "are still awaiting final rulemaking" [6] [press].
  • Category 1. Appendix B says each of the six was in FDA's interim Category 2 from 2023 "until April 22, 2026" [1] [primary]. None is in Category 1. The HHS draft is a separate policy.
  • Binding or permanent. The notice says the draft "does not establish any rights for any person and is not binding on HHS or the public" [2] [primary]. It gives no end date. It applies "until a peptide bulk drug substance is addressed in a final rule as being included or not included on the 503A bulks list" [1] [primary]. NCPA notes that "no timeframe was given" [6] [press].
  • Irrevocable. "HHS may revisit application of this interim policy (in whole or in part) if, among other things, a safety signal or product quality issue arises" [1][2] [primary].
  • A safety or efficacy finding. The documents contain no determination that any of the six is safe or effective. Appendix B records that for each peptide "CDER recommended against listing" and that the PCAC, which met 23–24 Jul 2026 [4], voted in favour [1] [primary]. The draft was reviewed by OIRA from 14 Oct to 27 Oct 2026 under the title "Interim Access Policy for Compounding Using Certain Peptides" [3] [primary]. NPR reports that FDA's own scientists recommended against unwinding the restrictions [5] [press].

The comment window is "2 weeks after date of publication in the Federal Register," through regulations.gov on docket HHS-OASH-2026-0496 [2] [primary].

Scope: forms, listed routes and single ingredient

The coverage is narrow. Appendix B defines each covered identity by amino acid sequence, formula and molecular weight [1] [primary]. The forms are BPC-157 acetate, TB-500 acetate, epitalon acetate, KPV acetate, MOTS-c acetate and semax free base. Other salt forms are not listed.

The draft also lists routes. The list below describes the policy's scope only. It is not usage information.

  • BPC-157 acetate: subcutaneous, intramuscular, oral and topical dosage forms
  • TB-500 acetate: subcutaneous or intramuscular injectable dosage forms only
  • MOTS-c acetate: subcutaneous or intramuscular injectable dosage forms
  • Epitalon acetate: subcutaneous or intramuscular injectable dosage forms "dispensed in intermittent courses"
  • Semax free base: intranasal use
  • KPV acetate: topical and oral dosage forms [1] [primary]

The product must contain "only a single Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient (API) listed in Appendix A" [1] [primary]. Blends fall outside the draft. That includes combinations of two listed peptides, such as BPC-157 with TB-500. The only drug delivery device that may be co-packaged with or contain the compounded drug is "an FDA 510(k)-cleared syringe" [1] [primary]. For any oral form, the compounder is expected to keep documentation showing "an adequate level of oral bioavailability in humans" [1] [primary].

Identity, purity and adverse-event conditions, as stated

The draft does not use the word "certify." These are the conditions in its own words [1] [primary]:

  • Identity. The substance "has the identity and limitations in route of administration described in Appendix B. The identity includes but is not limited to amino acid sequence, chemical structure, molecular weight, and molecular formula."
  • Characterization. The substance "is from a facility registered under section 510 … and characterized and identified in a valid certificate of analysis (COA) that includes test results consistent with existing guidance-based criteria described by FDA." HHS says this "helps provide assurance that what a compounder receives from a supplier is what it claims to be and has been tested for identity, purity, potency, and the absence of harmful contaminants such as endotoxins, heavy metals, microbial contamination, and impurities."
  • Original manufacturer. The original manufacturer, "not a subsequent packer, repacker, labeler, or distributor," must be registered under section 510 and comply with CGMP. Its facility location must be listed on the COA. An FDA-registered repacker or reseller must itself document "vendor validation" of the manufacturer and its COA. The COA requirements include the grade "Intended for human drug compounding."
  • Reporting. Compounders must "report products compounded, serious adverse events, and product quality issues to FDA and to the States where the products are compounded and sent (if different)." Serious adverse events must be reported "regardless of whether or not considered drug related," and product-quality issues as well, to FDA's MedWatch program. Product reports must include the active ingredient and its strength, the original manufacturer with its facility identifier, and the dosage form and route. The reporting procedure "should be detailed on the product labeling provided to the patient."
  • Label. The label must state: "This is a compounded drug product. Not for resale."
  • Other law. The product must comply with "all other applicable requirements of the FD&C Act," including the insanitary-conditions ban and "section 503A's … patient specific prescription requirement."

How this differs from RUO-labelled products

RUO ("research use only") products are sold with a label saying they are not for human use. The draft's conditions describe a different channel:

  • Labelling. Covered compounded products carry the statement "This is a compounded drug product. Not for resale" [1] [primary]. RUO products carry research-only labelling.
  • Intended use. The draft covers drug products compounded for an individual patient under section 503A [1] [primary]. RUO labelling states that a product is not intended for human use.
  • Prescription. The draft requires a valid patient-specific prescription [1] [primary]. No prescription is involved in RUO sales.
  • Identity and purity oversight. The draft ties coverage to a 510-registered, CGMP-compliant original manufacturer, a COA meeting FDA-referenced testing criteria, and MedWatch reporting [1] [primary]. RUO products are outside these terms, and none of the draft's identity, purity or reporting conditions apply to them.

HHS's stated rationale refers to RUO directly. The Secretary "has determined that this limited enforcement-discretion policy will discourage the continued, widespread use of certain research-use-only peptides supplied by foreign manufacturers that pose a safety risk to US patients" [1] [primary]. That is HHS's framing. The draft does not cover, authorise or legitimise RUO sales.

State-law note

The draft mentions States in its reporting condition and covers "State-licensed" pharmacies [1] [primary]. It contains no express statement about state pharmacy law. The law firm Frier Levitt writes that the policy "does not displace independent state pharmacy board requirements" and that pharmacies must still assess state law [7] [press]. That is the firm's analysis, not text from the policy.

Litigation context: Eli Lilly's retatrutide suits

On 12 Aug 2026, Eli Lilly announced six US lawsuits over unapproved retatrutide. Retatrutide is an investigational drug that Lilly says is in Phase 3 trials and not approved anywhere [8] [company-reported]. Lilly says the suits target "compounding pharmacies, medical spas, and online sellers that falsely claim their drugs are for 'research-use only' when they are actually intended for human use" [8] [company-reported]. The six cases it lists were filed in federal district courts in California and Texas [8] [company-reported]. Reuters reported the filings the same day [9] [press]. These are allegations, and no ruling is reported in these sources. Retatrutide is not one of the six peptides in the HHS draft.

FAQ

Did FDA approve these six peptides?

No. The notice comes from the HHS Office of the Secretary. It says compounded drugs are not FDA-approved, and none of the six is on the 503A Bulks List [1][2] [primary].

Is the policy final?

No. The Federal Register notice calls it a draft, says it is not binding, and opens a two-week comment window after publication on 30 Oct 2026 [2] [primary].

How long does it last?

No end date is given. It applies until a final rule addresses each substance, and HHS may revisit it at any time [1] [primary].

Does it cover blends such as BPC-157 with TB-500?

No. The draft requires a single listed active ingredient [1] [primary].

Does it cover RUO-labelled products?

No. Its terms depend on 503A compounding, a patient-specific prescription and registered CGMP sourcing. HHS calls foreign RUO peptides a safety risk [1] [primary].

Did FDA scientists support it?

Appendix B records that CDER recommended against listing each of the six and that the PCAC voted in favour [1] [primary].
